summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing territory with its own Parliament and its own Supreme Court, which between them make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply here of their own force: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council. No such extension appears in the sourced material.

No process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read in public and at the border under that marker.

Protection against discrimination on grounds of gender reassignment, alongside sexual orientation, has been in place since 2007. The Ministry for Justice and Equality is the department that has spoken publicly about bias-motivated abuse.

Hate-crime law is a live protection. An amendment to the Crimes Act 2011, passed on 19 September 2013, given royal assent on 25 September and in force on 10 October 2013, made hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation criminal offences. In July 2026 Parliament passed a further bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to bring transgender identity within those protections. Whether the 2026 provisions have been charged or prosecuted is not sourced here.

Conversion therapy is prohibited: in July 2026 Parliament passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practise it. A visitor considering local care should treat any offer of such practice as unlawful.

Relationship recognition is settled. Civil partnerships have existed since 2014 and same-sex marriage has been available since December 2016, when the enabling bill passed unanimously. A spouse or partner travelling with a trans visitor can be recognised as such under local law.

Social climate carries some documented friction. Following an incident of anti-gay abuse in July 2021, the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would consider legislation to tackle what Chief Minister Fabian Picardo called 'disgusting lurking homophobia' circulating on social media during Pride month.
tangentialFactors:
The United Kingdom's House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee set expectations for Gibraltar in its Seventh Report of 2007-08 on Overseas Territories, addressing accountability and good governance. Its 2008 inquiry recommended that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender status be made illegal across all overseas territories, a benchmark against which Gibraltar's own statutory protections can be read.

Reform has not always been smooth. The December 2015 consultation on amending the Civil Marriage Act left Gibraltarians polarised, according to El País in English (15 August 2016); an inter-ministerial committee under a government minister weighed the viewpoints, and the eventual bill passed Parliament in December 2016 with the support of the main parties. Legislative change on relationship law here has followed public consultation rather than judicial order, unlike the adoption reform of 2013.

The 2013 adoption change came from the courts rather than Parliament: on 10 April 2013 the Supreme Court of Gibraltar held that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, after a long-term lesbian couple challenged the refusal of an adoption for want of legal recognition of their relationship.
localsOnly:
Family law for residents has moved considerably. The government amended the adoption rules through the 2014 civil partnership legislation, and the Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024, expressly permitting same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination.

In February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law allowing non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination. In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority approved an amendment to its in vitro fertilisation policy giving lesbian couples access to assisted reproductive technology.

The age of consent stands at 16 for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender. The Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that the higher age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set the equal age of 16 with effect from 23 November 2012; before that gay male minors faced 18, and a private member's bill to equalise consent was defeated on 18 May 2009. Same-sex conduct has been legal since 1993 and the age of consent equalised in law since 2012; adoption by same-sex couples was permitted by the 2013 Supreme Court ruling.

In July 2021 the Ministry for Justice and Equality began investigating a proposal to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence. The sourced material does not record whether that proposal was enacted.

Unresolved: the sourced material does not state whether the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 or its 2025 single-sex-services code has at any point been extended to Gibraltar by Order in Council, nor whether any application of those instruments by local ordinance exists.

Unresolved: no penalty, sentencing range or enforcement record is sourced for the 2013 sexual-orientation hate-crime offences, the July 2026 transgender-identity additions to hate crime and hate speech law, or the July 2026 conversion therapy offence. Charging and prosecution data are absent.

Unresolved: the inventory contains no record of pending or draft gender-recognition legislation, and no record of how border officials, airlines or police handle a document whose marker does not match presentation. The 2007 discrimination protection is reported through encyclopedic sources rather than the text of the statute itself.

Several claims rest on Wikipedia-derived mirrors, which are convenient summaries but not primary legal texts; the statute citations and dates they carry should be verified against the published laws of Gibraltar before being relied on.
